Featured case study

Jersey City Last-Mile Mobility Analysis

Which CitiBike stations run out of bikes, when, and for whom? An analysis of 94,689 trips across Jersey City and Hoboken, from raw data to a rebalancing plan.

Jun 2026 - Jul 2026PostgreSQL · Python (pandas, matplotlib, seaborn) · Tableau

94,689
verified trips
108
stations mapped
10
priority stations
17.8%
peak daily imbalance

The question

How do CitiBike usage patterns in the Jersey City area reveal opportunities to better serve commuter and recreational demand?

The approach

Cleaned 95,350 raw trips in pandas, removing 355 null records and 306 cross-system rides to leave 94,689. Built reusable PostgreSQL views for each station's daily bike flow and imbalance, kept low-volume noise out of the rankings with a reliability filter (more than 25 daily rides on at least 6 of 31 days), and published a Tableau map of every station.

Finding 01

Members commute. Casual riders don't.

Members take short trips at high volume nearly all day, with peaks in the morning and evening. Casual riders ride longer and build to a single evening peak, with no morning spike at all.

Member8 min
Casual15 min

Average ride length

Finding 02

Bike drain concentrates in one corridor.

Oakland Ave, McGinley Square, and Glenwood Ave lose the most bikes every day, and the draining stations cluster in a single Jersey City corridor. Surplus stations such as River St & Newark St and City Hall split evenly across both cities.

The recommendation

Split rebalancing by city, not by operation type. Every draining and surplus station sorts cleanly into Jersey City or Hoboken, so one route per city covers the whole problem without cross-city travel. Shared transit hubs like Grove St PATH should be sized for peak-hour capacity, not all-day demand.

How the numbers were checked

I used Claude as an independent code reviewer to reproduce the results. It surfaced a NULL-handling bug and a sign error affecting 44 of 81 stations, both fixed before publishing.
